2- **Confirmation Bias**: This is a cognitive bias where people tend to search for, interpret, favor, and recall information in a way that confirms their pre-existing beliefs or hypotheses. Instead of objectively evaluating all available information, individuals unconsciously seek out evidence that supports what they already believe and dismiss or downplay information that contradicts it. For example, if someone believes a particular political candidate is corrupt, they will more readily notice and remember news stories that highlight the candidate's missteps, while ignoring positive reports. Understanding confirmation bias helps us recognize our own tendencies to selectively see what we want to see, encouraging us to actively seek out diverse perspectives and evidence, especially that which challenges our own views, to make more balanced and informed decisions.

While people try countless home remedies or breathing techniques, hiccups are an involuntary reflex caused by a spasm of the diaphragm and rapid closure of the vocal cords, controlled by a complex reflex arc in the brainstem. You cannot simply "will" your diaphragm to stop spasming. Many people might think holding their breath or drinking water will immediately solve it, but the body's deep-seated autonomic reflex is much tougher to defy than people assume, often requiring the reflex to run its course.

2- **Cognitive Dissonance** is the mental discomfort (psychological stress) experienced by a person who holds two or more contradictory beliefs, ideas, or values; or participates in an action that goes against one of their beliefs, ideas, or values. For example, a person who believes strongly in environmental protection but drives a gas-guzzling SUV might experience cognitive dissonance. To reduce this discomfort, they might change their belief (e.g., decide environmental issues aren't that serious), change their behavior (buy an electric car), or more commonly, rationalize their behavior (e.g., "I need this car for safety," or "my one car won't make a difference"). Understanding cognitive dissonance helps explain why people rationalize their decisions, resist contradictory information, and often change their attitudes to match their actions, even when those actions might be regrettable.
